extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: MathQA is a large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems covering multiple math domain categories, annotated with formal operation programs. It significantly enhances the AQuA dataset with fully-specified operational programs using a new operation-based representation language.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI)
extraction.citeAs: Amini et al. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Math word problems were sourced from the AQuA dataset and annotated with formal operation programs using a dynamic crowd-sourcing annotation platform. Problems were first categorized into math domains, then crowd workers iteratively selected operations and arguments to build operation programs. Quality control was enforced through test questions and validation by at least 2 out of 3 validators.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The AQuA (AQUA-RAT) dataset, which provides over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems with multiple-choice options.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion was performed by finding closely similar problems, replacing numeric values with generic numbers, and expanding annotations to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were filtered for solvability: unsolvable problems (no words, sequence problems, requiring options, non-numeric) and duplicates were identified. Math problems were categorized into math domains using term frequencies to prune the search space of possible operations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers used a dynamic annotation platform to annotate math word problems with formal operation programs. Annotators iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. Programs were only accepted if they included numbers from the problem and whose final calculation was close to the correct numeric solution. Quality control was enforced through randomly evaluated test questions with an accuracy threshold. Alignment validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank the operation program as valid.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems shows 92% of annotations are valid, with 87% agreement between expert validation and crowd-sourcing validation. Annotators were dynamically evaluated through quality-control questions and had to maintain an accuracy threshold; if accuracy dropped below threshold, previous annotations were labeled as untrusted.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 (2 out of 3 validators required to validate each annotation)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automatic dynamic programming approach was also experimented with to generate operation programs using numbers in the AQuA rationales, but was not included in the final dataset due to noise.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The AQuA dataset contains significant noise including problems with incorrect solutions, problems unsolvable without brute-force, and rationales with missing steps. Many problems are near-duplicates with slight changes not reflected in rationales. The categorization strategy may be noisy due to use of only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: High-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely nonnumeric are omitted. The dataset does not cover sequence problems, factorization, and other advanced math domains. The representation language has 58 operations and cannot represent all problem types. Results are significantly lower than human performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of neural math word problem solvers. The dataset is split 80/12/8% for training/dev/test. It can be used for benchmarking interpretable math problem solving models.
